For a stable, externally reachable address, attach the VM to a VLAN or untagged network. A Kubernetes Service object can also give a stable IP on the management network.

instruction: Can clients outside the cluster reach a VM on the SUSE Virtualization management network?
output: Not by default. The management network IP of a VM can be reached only from within the cluster nodes. Use a VLAN network or untagged network for VMs that must connect to the external network.

instruction: What MTU do VM interfaces get on the mgmt network?
output: VM interfaces connected to `mgmt` get an MTU of 1450, even though `mgmt` itself typically uses 1500. The 50-byte difference is the overhead of the Calico and Flannel (Canal) overlay that carries the in-cluster network. If your workloads depend on a specific MTU, set appropriate values on the affected interfaces and bridges.

instruction: Large packets from a VM on the default network get dropped but small ones work. What is likely going on?
output: VMs on the management network have an interface MTU of 1450, not 1500, because the Calico/Flannel overlay adds 50 bytes per packet. Traffic sized for a 1500 MTU will not fit. Adjust the MTU in the guest, or use a VLAN network, which inherits the MTU of its cluster network configuration.

instruction: I installed Harvester with MTU 9000 on the management interface. Do I need to do anything else?
output: Yes. Annotate the `mgmt` cluster network with the same value: `kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000"`. Without the annotation, VM networks on `mgmt` use the default MTU 1500 instead of inheriting your value. The annotation must match the `mtu` set in `install.management_interface`, and all nodes must use the same MTU.

instruction: Give me just the command to set the uplink MTU annotation on mgmt to 9000.
output: `kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000"`

instruction: VM networks on mgmt still show MTU 1500 although our management bond is jumbo. Why?
output: SUSE Virtualization needs an annotation on the `mgmt` cluster network when the installed MTU is not 0 or 1500. Run `kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000"` (use your actual MTU). After that, VM networks attached to `mgmt` inherit the value. Make sure every node uses the same MTU.

instruction: After changing the mgmt MTU with nmcli on all nodes, what's the last step so VM networks pick it up?
output: Annotate the `mgmt` cluster network with the new value, for example `kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000"`. VM networks attached to `mgmt` then inherit the new MTU. Before that, stop the VMs attached to `mgmt` and verify the new MTU with `ip link`.

instruction: How do I create a VM in SUSE Virtualization?
output: Open the Virtual Machines page and click Create. Pick a namespace and a VM name, then set CPU, memory and SSH keys on the Basics tab. Select an image on the Volumes tab (the first disk is the root disk) and configure networks on the Networks tab, where the management network is added by default. Cloud-init data, run strategy and OS type are under Advanced Options.

instruction: Which namespace should I use if every Harvester user needs to see a VM?
output: Use `harvester-public`. When creating a VM in SUSE Virtualization (Harvester), it is the only namespace that is visible to all users.

instruction: When I add several disks to a new VM, which one boots?
output: On the Volumes tab, the first disk is the root disk by default. You can change the boot order by dragging and dropping volumes or with the arrow buttons. For an ISO install, place the empty volume above the cd-rom image so the VM boots from disk after installation.

instruction: Walk me through the tabs of the Harvester VM create form.
output: Basics holds CPU, memory and SSH keys. Volumes holds the image and additional disks, with the first disk as root. Networks attaches the management network (added by default) or VLAN networks. Node Scheduling and VM Scheduling set affinity rules, and Advanced Options covers run strategy, OS type and cloud-init.

instruction: What is the default run strategy for VMs in Harvester?
output: The default is `RerunOnFailure`. The VM instance is respawned only if it failed in an error state. If the guest shuts down cleanly from inside, it is not recreated.

instruction: I shut down a VM from inside the guest and it stayed off. Is that expected?
output: Yes, with the default `RerunOnFailure` run strategy. A successful guest shutdown is not restarted; only failures are respawned. Use `Always` if you want the instance to be recreated whenever it stops.

instruction: What run strategies exist in SUSE Virtualization and what do they do?
output: There are four. `Always` always keeps an instance and respawns it after a crash. `RerunOnFailure` (the default) respawns only after an error and leaves a clean shutdown off. `Manual` creates or removes the instance only through start, stop and restart actions. `Stop` means no instance runs.

instruction: Which run strategy should I use so a critical VM comes back even after someone powers it off from inside?
output: Use `Always`. With `Always`, the VM instance always exists and is respawned if it stops or crashes. The default, `RerunOnFailure`, does not restart a VM that was shut down cleanly from inside the guest.

instruction: How can I add a VM image to Harvester?
output: There are three ways. Download it from a URL the cluster can reach, upload a local file (qcow2, raw and ISO are supported), or create it from an existing volume with Export Image on the Volumes page. When uploading through the browser, do not refresh the page until the upload is finished.

instruction: Is it OK to use the Ubuntu daily cloud image URL for a SUSE Virtualization image?
output: Avoid it. If all replicas of a SUSE Storage (Longhorn) backing image are lost, Longhorn downloads the URL again to self-heal. A daily-build URL serves different content over time, which causes a checksum mismatch and lost replicas. Use a fixed, versioned image URL.

instruction: Which image formats can I upload from my workstation to SUSE Virtualization?
output: Local uploads support qcow2, raw and ISO images. You can also create images from a URL the cluster can reach, or by exporting an existing volume.

instruction: How do I turn an existing VM disk into a reusable image in Harvester?
output: On the Volumes page, select the volume and use Export Image. Enter the image name and select a StorageClass. The new image can then be used to create other VMs.

instruction: My new VM shows no IP address in the Harvester UI. How do I check why?
output: Check whether the QEMU guest agent is reporting: `kubectl get vmi -n <NAMESPACE> <NAME> -ojsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].infoSource}'`. If the output does not contain `guest-agent`, the `qemu-guest-agent` package is not installed. Fix it under Edit Config > Advanced Options > Cloud Config by selecting Install guest agent.

instruction: Command only: check if a VMI's interface info comes from the guest agent.
output: `kubectl get vmi -n <NAMESPACE> <NAME> -ojsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].infoSource}'`

instruction: An imported VM in SUSE Virtualization never displays its IP. What's the usual cause and how do I confirm it?
output: The usual cause is a missing `qemu-guest-agent` package in the guest. Confirm with `kubectl get vmi -n <NAMESPACE> <NAME> -ojsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].infoSource}'`; the output lacks `guest-agent` when the agent is not installed. Install the agent with the Install guest agent option in the VM's Cloud Config.

instruction: How do I verify the QEMU guest agent is working for a Harvester VM from kubectl?
output: Run `kubectl get vmi -n <NAMESPACE> <NAME> -ojsonpath='{.status.interfaces[0].infoSource}'`. When the agent reports interface data, the output includes `guest-agent`. If it does not, install `qemu-guest-agent`, for example with Install guest agent in Cloud Config.

instruction: I enabled Install guest agent on an existing Harvester VM but nothing changed. Why?
output: cloud-init runs only once, when the VM boots for the first time, so new Cloud Config settings are not applied automatically. Inside the guest, run `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/*`, then restart the VM. cloud-init then runs again and installs `qemu-guest-agent`.

instruction: How do I force cloud-init to run again on a SUSE Virtualization VM?
output: Delete the cloud-init state directory inside the guest with `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/*`, then restart the VM. cloud-init normally runs only on the first boot, so this is required after editing the VM's Cloud Config.

instruction: Just the command to clear cloud-init state inside a guest.
output: `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/*` Restart the VM afterwards so cloud-init runs again.

instruction: I edited the user data of a running VM in Harvester to add packages. What do I do so it takes effect?
output: Run `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/*` inside the guest, then restart the VM. cloud-init only runs on first boot, so without clearing that directory the new Cloud Config is ignored.

instruction: How do I live-migrate a VM in Harvester?
output: On the Virtual Machines page, find the VM and select ⋮ > Migrate. Choose the target node and click Apply. Live migration moves the running VM to another host without downtime.

instruction: The Migrate option is missing for one of my SUSE Virtualization VMs. Why?
output: Migrate is not offered when the cluster has only one node, when the VM is non-migratable (for example it has PCI or vGPU passthrough or is bound to one node), or when the VM already has a running or pending migration. Fix the cause and the option returns.

instruction: How do I cancel a live migration that is taking too long?
output: On the Virtual Machines page, select ⋮ > Abort Migration for the migrating VM. The item is available while a migration is running or pending. Do not use it for migrations created by batch migration during maintenance or upgrades.

instruction: Is live migration in SUSE Virtualization done from the host page or the VM page?
output: From the Virtual Machines page: select the VM, then ⋮ > Migrate, pick the target node and click Apply. To evacuate all VMs from a host at once, use Maintenance Mode on the host instead.

instruction: Which VMs can't be live-migrated in Harvester?
output: VMs with host device passthrough (PCI, vGPU or USB devices), VMs pinned to a specific node with a node selector, and VMs whose scheduling rules match only one node cannot be live-migrated. Examples of the last case are a VM attached to a cluster network that covers only one node, or CPU pinning when CPU Manager is enabled on only one node. Remove the non-migratable devices or add schedulable nodes to make the VM migratable.

instruction: Can I live-migrate a VM that has a GPU passed through?
output: No. In SUSE Virtualization, host device passthrough such as PCI and vGPU makes a VM non-migratable, because the device belongs to a specific node. Shut such VMs down before host maintenance.

instruction: Maintenance mode won't activate on my node. What could block it?
output: Non-migratable VMs on the node can prevent Maintenance Mode from activating. These include VMs with PCI, vGPU or USB passthrough, VMs bound to that node with a node selector, and VMs whose scheduling rules match only that node. Identify those VMs and shut them down manually.

instruction: I pinned a VM to node harv21 with a node selector. Does that affect migration?
output: Yes. A node selector that binds a VM to a specific node makes it non-migratable in SUSE Virtualization. Use scheduling rules that match a group of nodes if you need the VM to stay live-migratable.

instruction: Why did a live migration of a busy VM get aborted in Harvester?
output: Live migration is aborted when it exceeds the completion timeout, 150 seconds per GiB of data by default, or when memory copying makes no progress for 150 seconds. A VM that dirties memory faster than it can be copied hits these limits. Adjust `completionTimeoutPerGiB` and `progressTimeout` in the `kubevirt-migration` setting, or enable `allowAutoConverge`.

instruction: How long can a migration of an 8 GiB VM run before SUSE Virtualization cancels it?
output: 1200 seconds by default. The completion timeout is 150 seconds per GiB, so 8 GiB × 150 s = 1200 s. A separate progress timeout aborts the migration if memory copying makes no progress for 150 seconds.

instruction: What setting controls live migration timeouts in SUSE Virtualization?
output: Use the cluster-wide `kubevirt-migration` setting. `completionTimeoutPerGiB` (default 150) sets the seconds allowed per GiB, and `progressTimeout` (default 150) sets how long a migration may run without progress. Instead of raising timeouts, consider `allowAutoConverge`, which lets KubeVirt throttle the guest CPU so the migration can finish.

instruction: A write-heavy database VM never finishes migrating. Should I just raise the timeout?
output: The docs suggest enabling `allowAutoConverge` in the `kubevirt-migration` setting before increasing the timeout. It lets KubeVirt throttle the guest CPU when memory changes faster than it can be copied, which makes completion more likely. The defaults are a 150 s per GiB completion timeout and a 150 s progress timeout.

instruction: Should I edit the kubevirt CR directly to tune migrations in Harvester?
output: No. Since v1.7.0, configure live migration through the `kubevirt-migration` setting rather than editing the `kubevirt` object. The entire JSON value of the setting is applied to `spec.configuration.migrations`, so direct edits are overwritten the next time the setting is saved.

instruction: Where do I set parallel migrations per cluster in SUSE Virtualization?
output: In the `kubevirt-migration` setting, field `parallelMigrationsPerCluster` (default 5). The same setting holds `parallelOutboundMigrationsPerNode` (default 2), `bandwidthPerMigration`, the timeouts and other options. Wait until active migrations finish before saving changes.

instruction: Is it safe to change kubevirt-migration during a maintenance window with migrations running?
output: No. Do not modify the `kubevirt-migration` setting while migrations are in progress; wait until all active migrations have finished. When you save it, every field in the JSON is written to the `kubevirt` object, including fields you did not change.

instruction: I changed migration parameters with kubectl edit on the kubevirt object and they got reverted. Why?
output: SUSE Virtualization manages migration configuration through the `kubevirt-migration` setting. Its whole JSON value is applied to `spec.configuration.migrations` of the `kubevirt` object, overwriting changes made directly there. Make your changes in the setting instead.

instruction: My VMs can't migrate between two nodes with different CPU models. How do I fix it cluster-wide?
output: Run `kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system` and add `spec.configuration.cpuModel` with a CPU model that all nodes support (for example `"123"` if every node has the label `cpu-model.node.kubevirt.io/123`). This also applies to new VMs. Existing VMs must be restarted to pick up the model.

instruction: What command lets me set a default CPU model for all Harvester VMs?
output: `kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system`, then add `spec.configuration.cpuModel: "<model>"`. Choose a model listed in the `cpu-model.node.kubevirt.io/<model>` labels of every node. Restart VMs for the change to take effect.

instruction: Why does host-model block migration in SUSE Virtualization, and what can I do?
output: With `host-model` (the default when no CPU model is set), a VM can only migrate to a node with the same primary CPU model. To fix this cluster-wide, run `kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system` and set `spec.configuration.cpuModel` to a model all nodes support. For one VM, set `spec.template.spec.domain.cpu.model` instead. Both approaches need a VM restart.

instruction: Just the command to edit the KubeVirt CR for a cluster CPU model.
output: `kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system` Add `spec.configuration.cpuModel`, then restart the affected VMs.

instruction: How do I put a Harvester node into maintenance?
output: On the Hosts page, select ⋮ > Enable Maintenance Mode for the node. SUSE Virtualization uses batch migration to move live-migratable VMs to other nodes. You need at least two active nodes. Non-migratable VMs can block activation and must be shut down manually.

instruction: I want one VM to just shut down instead of migrating when its node enters maintenance. How?
output: Add the label `harvesterhci.io/maintain-mode-strategy` with the value `Shutdown` to the VM. Other values are `Migrate` (the default), `ShutdownAndRestartAfterEnable` (restarted on a different node once the node is in maintenance), and `ShutdownAndRestartAfterDisable` (restarted on the same node when maintenance ends).

instruction: What does ShutdownAndRestartAfterDisable do in SUSE Virtualization?
output: It is a value of the `harvesterhci.io/maintain-mode-strategy` VM label. The VM is shut down when Maintenance Mode is enabled and restarted when Maintenance Mode is disabled, so it stays on the same node. Without the label, the default behavior is `Migrate`.

instruction: Can I use maintenance mode on a single-node Harvester cluster?
output: No. Maintenance Mode needs at least two active nodes, because it evacuates VMs by live-migrating them to other nodes. On a single node you must shut the VMs down yourself.

instruction: Where do I configure the backup target in Harvester?
output: Go to Settings > backup-target. Choose type NFS or S3. For S3 set the endpoint (optional), bucket name, bucket region and access keys, plus a certificate if the server is self-signed. For NFS set the endpoint URL. VM backups cannot be created until a backup target is set.

instruction: What kinds of storage can SUSE Virtualization use as a backup target?
output: An NFS server or an S3-compatible server. You configure it at Settings > backup-target. VM backup volumes are stored there and can restore a new VM or replace an existing one.

instruction: Can I back up a VM whose disks are on a third-party CSI storage class?
output: No. Backup support is limited to SUSE Storage (Longhorn) volumes, and SUSE Virtualization cannot create backups of volumes in external storage. Use your storage vendor's tools to protect those volumes.

instruction: The Take Backup action prompts me to set something first. What is missing?
output: A backup target. Configure Settings > backup-target with an NFS or S3-compatible endpoint, then run Take Backup again from the Virtual Machines page.

instruction: What's the difference between a VM backup and a VM snapshot in Harvester?
output: A backup (Take Backup) stores the VM's volumes on the external backup target (NFS or S3). It can restore a new VM, replace an existing one, or restore on another cluster configured with the same backup target. A snapshot (Take VM Snapshot) is stored inside the cluster and works without a backup target. Use backups for disaster recovery off the cluster.

instruction: How do I restore a SUSE Virtualization VM backup on a different cluster?
output: Configure the same backup target on the new cluster. The backup controller syncs the backup metadata automatically. Then go to VM Backups, select the synced backup and restore it as a new VM with a name you specify. From v1.4.0, VM images are synced to the new cluster automatically, unless an image with the same name or display name already exists.

instruction: I tried Replace Existing from a backup and it won't proceed. Why?
output: Replacing an existing VM from a backup requires the VM to exist and be powered off. Stop the VM, then go to VM Backups > Restore Backup > Replace Existing. By default the previous volumes are deleted, but you can choose to keep them.

instruction: Do VM snapshots in SUSE Virtualization protect me if the whole cluster is lost?
output: No. VM snapshots are stored in the cluster itself. For protection against losing the cluster, use VM backups, which go to an external NFS or S3 backup target and can be restored on another cluster with the same backup target.

instruction: My restored Ubuntu VM got the same IP as the original. Why?
output: Ubuntu releases after 16.04 use netplan, which uses the machine ID as the DHCP client identifier. The restored VM keeps the original machine ID, so DHCP gives it the same address. Before taking backups or snapshots, set `dhcp-identifier: mac` under the interface (for example `enp1s0`) in the VM's network configuration.

instruction: What should I change on Ubuntu VMs before using Harvester backups?
output: Stop the VM, open Edit Config > Advanced Options, and set the netplan network data to use `dhcp4: true` and `dhcp-identifier: mac` on the interface. Then restart the VM. Without this, a VM restored from a backup or snapshot gets the same DHCP IP as the original.

instruction: Is there anything special about snapshotting Ubuntu guests in SUSE Virtualization?
output: Yes. Configure netplan with `dhcp-identifier: mac` first. Otherwise the restored VM, which keeps the original machine ID, receives the same IP address from the DHCP server. That can cause network conflicts if both VMs run.

instruction: We cloned a VM from a backup and now two VMs fight over one IP. How do we prevent this next time?
output: Before creating backups or snapshots of netplan-based Ubuntu VMs (releases after 16.04), set `dhcp-identifier: mac` in the VM's network configuration. netplan otherwise uses the machine ID, which the restored VM keeps, as the DHCP client identifier, so both VMs get the same IP.

instruction: How do I schedule regular VM backups in Harvester?
output: Go to Virtual Machine Schedules and click Create Schedule. Choose Backup or Snapshot, set the namespace and VM, a cron schedule, Retain (how many to keep) and Max Failure (consecutive failures allowed before the schedule is suspended). The interval must be at least one hour. This is available from v1.4.0.

instruction: Can I take a VM snapshot every 15 minutes with SUSE Virtualization schedules?
output: No. The backup or snapshot interval must be at least one hour, because frequent deletion of backups and snapshots causes heavy I/O. If two schedules have the same granularity, their timing offset must be at least 10 minutes.

instruction: Should I use Longhorn recurring jobs for VM backups on Harvester?
output: No. SUSE Virtualization does not support Longhorn recurring snapshot and backup jobs; they conflict with operations such as VM attachment and upgrades and can generate heavy I/O. Use Virtual Machine Schedules, which include safeguards.

instruction: My VM backup schedule stopped running by itself. What happened?
output: A schedule is suspended automatically when consecutive failed attempts exceed its Max Failure value, for example while the backup target is unreachable. Fix the cause, ideally confirm with a manual backup, then resume the schedule with ⋮ > Suspend or Resume on the Virtual Machine Schedules screen.

instruction: How do I test whether a VM supports filesystem freeze for Harvester backups?
output: Exec into the `compute` container of the VM's virt-launcher pod, then run `virt-freezer --freeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` and check the result. Always thaw afterwards with `virt-freezer --unfreeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` before doing anything else. The freeze needs the QEMU guest agent in the guest.

instruction: Command only: freeze a VM's filesystems with virt-freezer.
output: `virt-freezer --freeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` Run it inside the virt-launcher `compute` container, and thaw with `--unfreeze` afterwards.

instruction: Snapshots of a RHEL VM fail with 'Failed to freeze filesystem'. How do I reproduce it manually?
output: Open a shell in the VM's virt-launcher `compute` container and run `virt-freezer --freeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>`. A SELinux `Permission denied` for `guest-fsfreeze-freeze` points to a missing custom SELinux policy for `qemu-ga`. Thaw the VM with `virt-freezer --unfreeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` when done.

instruction: Where is virt-freezer and what do I run to check freeze support in SUSE Virtualization?
output: virt-freezer is available in the `compute` container of the VM's virt-launcher pod. Run `virt-freezer --freeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>` there and verify the result, then thaw with `virt-freezer --unfreeze --namespace <VM namespace> --name <VM name>`. Windows guests need the VSS service for freeze to work.

instruction: Can I upgrade SUSE Virtualization from v1.6 directly to v1.8?
output: No. The supported paths move one minor version at a time: v1.6.x to v1.7.x, then v1.7.x to v1.8.x. You can skip patch releases within that path, for example going straight to the latest v1.7 patch. Downgrades are not supported.

instruction: What order should I upgrade Rancher and Harvester in?
output: If Rancher manages your SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) cluster, upgrade Rancher first, then upgrade SUSE Virtualization. The two upgrades are independent; the cluster stays reachable through its VIP during the Rancher upgrade and is not upgraded automatically.

instruction: Can I roll back a Harvester upgrade if something goes wrong?
output: No. SUSE Virtualization does not support downgrades, to avoid problems from incompatible, deprecated or removed functions. Back up VMs before upgrading and follow the supported paths.

instruction: Where do I start an upgrade in SUSE Virtualization?
output: Click Upgrade on the Dashboard screen of the UI. The button appears when a version you can upgrade to is available. Then select the target version and follow progress with the circle indicator. For air-gapped clusters you can import the ISO under Advanced > Settings > server-version > Upgrade (v1.8.0 and later).

instruction: How much free disk space do Harvester nodes need before an upgrade?
output: Each node needs at least 30 GiB of free system partition space. Check it with `df -h /usr/local/`. If any node has less than 30 GiB, the upgrade is denied.

instruction: Command to check the system partition free space before a SUSE Virtualization upgrade?
output: `df -h /usr/local/` Every node needs at least 30 GiB free.

instruction: My SUSE Virtualization upgrade was refused for disk space. What do I check?
output: Run `df -h /usr/local/` on every node; each needs at least 30 GiB free on the system partition. You can free space by cleaning up unused container images, for example with `crictl rmi --prune`, before retrying.

instruction: Pre-upgrade checklist item: how do I verify node disk headroom in Harvester?
output: On each node, run `df -h /usr/local/` and confirm at least 30 GiB is free on the system partition. Also run the pre-check script on a control-plane node, make sure node clocks are in sync, and back up VMs if needed.

instruction: My Harvester upgrade says a node will exceed the kubelet image garbage collection threshold of 85%. What do I do?
output: Clean up unused container images on that node with `crictl rmi --prune`, then start a new upgrade. The check exists because the kubelet deletes unused images above 85% disk usage, which could remove the newly preloaded images, especially in air-gapped clusters.

instruction: Give me just the command to prune unused images on a SUSE Virtualization node.
output: `crictl rmi --prune`

instruction: Why does SUSE Virtualization block an upgrade when image storage is above 85%?
output: The kubelet's default `imageGCHighThresholdPercent` is 85, so above that it removes unused images, including new images preloaded for the upgrade. In air-gapped environments that can break the upgrade. Free space with `crictl rmi --prune` on the affected node and retry.

instruction: Upgrade precheck failed: 'will reach 92.84% storage space after loading new images'. Fix?
output: Run `crictl rmi --prune` on the node named in the message to remove unused images, then start the upgrade again.

instruction: What does restoreVM in upgrade-config do?
output: `restoreVM` decides what happens to non-migratable VMs during an upgrade. With `true`, SUSE Virtualization shuts down running and paused non-migratable VMs and restarts the previously running ones after the upgrade completes successfully. With `false` (the default), you must stop non-migratable VMs yourself in multi-node clusters, and they are not restarted afterwards.

instruction: My upgrade is stuck because a GPU VM is still running. What are my options?
output: A VM with GPU passthrough is non-migratable. With the default `upgrade-config` value `restoreVM: false`, you must stop it manually before the upgrade can continue. Alternatively, set `restoreVM` to `true` before upgrading so SUSE Virtualization shuts such VMs down and restores them after the upgrade.

instruction: Will Harvester restart VMs I shut down manually before the upgrade?
output: No. `restoreVM` only applies to non-migratable VMs that SUSE Virtualization powers off automatically. VMs you shut down manually are not powered on after the upgrade; start them yourself, in batches to avoid a boot storm.

instruction: What happens to normal VMs during a SUSE Virtualization upgrade?
output: Live-migratable VMs are migrated to other nodes through batch migration before each node is upgraded, so they have no downtime. Non-migratable VMs are handled according to `restoreVM` in the `upgrade-config` setting.

instruction: How do I stop an upgrade that is in progress in Harvester?
output: Log in to a control-plane node and become root with `sudo -i`. List the ongoing upgrade with `kubectl get upgrade.harvesterhci.io -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/latestUpgrade=true`, then delete that `Upgrade` CR (for example `kubectl delete upgrade.harvesterhci.io/hvst-upgrade-9gmg2 -n harvester-system`). Finally, resume any ManagedCharts that the upgrade paused. Generate a support bundle first.

instruction: Command to find the current Upgrade object in SUSE Virtualization?
output: `kubectl get upgrade.harvesterhci.io -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/latestUpgrade=true`

instruction: An upgrade failed during image preloading and I want to restart it. What are the steps?
output: Generate a support bundle, then stop the upgrade. To stop it, list the CR with `kubectl get upgrade.harvesterhci.io -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/latestUpgrade=true`, delete it, and resume paused ManagedCharts. Then click Upgrade on the Dashboard again. Do not do this for failures in Phase 4 (node upgrades) unless SUSE Support tells you to.

instruction: What gets left paused when you manually stop a SUSE Virtualization upgrade?
output: ManagedCharts can stay paused, because the upgrade pauses them to avoid data races. After you list the Upgrade CR with `kubectl get upgrade.harvesterhci.io -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/latestUpgrade=true` and delete it, patch the charts (`harvester`, `harvester-crd`, `rancher-monitoring-crd`, `rancher-logging-crd` in `fleet-local`) back to `paused: false`.

instruction: How do I see which nodes are being upgraded in Harvester?
output: Run `kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node`. Each node gets a `pre-drain` job, which live-migrates or shuts down VMs and then upgrades RKE2, and a `post-drain` job, which upgrades and reboots the OS. Check logs with `kubectl logs -n harvester-system jobs/<job-name>`.

instruction: My SUSE Virtualization upgrade is stuck upgrading nodes. Can I just restart it?
output: No. If the upgrade fails or is stuck in Phase 4 (Upgrade Nodes), do not restart it unless SUSE Support instructs you to. Collect information with `kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node` and the job logs, generate a support bundle, and contact SUSE Support.

instruction: Command only: list the node upgrade jobs.
output: `kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node`

instruction: What jobs run on each node during a Harvester upgrade, and how do I list them?
output: In multi-node clusters each node runs a `pre-drain` job and a `post-drain` job; single-node clusters use a `single-node-upgrade` job. List them with `kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node`. If something fails at this phase, do not restart the upgrade without SUSE Support guidance.

instruction: What is a witness node in Harvester?
output: A witness node is limited to being an etcd cluster member. It helps keep etcd quorum but stores no data and runs no user workloads. SUSE Virtualization supports two management nodes plus one witness node, optionally with worker nodes. Only one witness node is allowed per cluster.

instruction: Can I turn an existing worker node into a witness node?
output: No. The witness role can be assigned only when the node joins the cluster, by choosing Witness Role in the installer. Each cluster can have only one witness node.

instruction: What runs on a SUSE Virtualization witness node?
output: Only essential workloads: harvester-node-manager, cloud-controller-manager, etcd, kube-proxy, rke2-canal and rke2-multus. SUSE Storage (Longhorn) is not provisioned there, because witness nodes store no data. etcd hardware recommendations still apply.

instruction: How small can a Harvester witness node be?
output: The requirements list a 180 GB minimum disk for witness nodes, and witness nodes do not need extra NICs for custom cluster networks. Because the witness runs etcd, follow etcd hardware recommendations; under-sized hardware significantly hurts cluster performance.

instruction: My volumes show Degraded in a Harvester cluster with a witness node. Why?
output: Witness nodes store no data, so a cluster with two management nodes and one witness can place only two replicas per volume. The default `harvester-longhorn` StorageClass asks for 3 replicas, so Longhorn marks volumes Degraded. Create a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2.

instruction: What StorageClass should I use for a 2+1 witness SUSE Virtualization cluster?
output: Create a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2. The built-in `harvester-longhorn` StorageClass uses 3 replicas, which cannot be met with only two data-storing nodes. If you add one or more worker nodes, the existing default StorageClass works.

instruction: I already created volumes with harvester-longhorn on a witness cluster. How do I fix them?
output: Change the replica count of those volumes on the Volume screen of the embedded Longhorn UI. Then create a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2 for future volumes, since the default `harvester-longhorn` uses 3.

instruction: Does the replica count matter if my witness cluster also has worker nodes?
output: With two management nodes, one witness and one or more worker nodes, you can keep the existing default StorageClass. Only the layout without workers (two management nodes plus one witness) needs a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2.

instruction: Live migration to one node always fails in my witness cluster. Why?
output: Check whether you are selecting the witness node as the target. The migration target list can include the witness node, but it runs no VMs, so migrating to it fails. Choose a management or worker node instead.

instruction: Why does the Harvester Migrate dialog show my witness node?
output: It is a known issue: the target list includes the witness node. Do not select it, because VM migration to the witness node fails. Pick one of the nodes that run workloads.

instruction: Is it safe to pick any node in the migration target list in a cluster with a witness?
output: No. In SUSE Virtualization the list may include the witness node, and selecting it makes the migration fail. Select only management or worker nodes.

instruction: What's the gotcha with witness nodes and VM migration?
output: The witness node can show up as a migration target even though it only runs etcd and essential components. Do not select it as the migration target, or the migration will fail.

instruction: How do I pass a GPU through to a VM in Harvester?
output: First enable the `pcidevices-controller` add-on. Then go to Advanced > PCI Devices, find the GPU (for example by searching NVIDIA), select it and click Enable Passthrough. Attach it under the VM's Edit Config > PCI Devices and click Save. Restart the VM immediately, then install the GPU driver inside the guest.

instruction: What driver does SUSE Virtualization bind passthrough devices to?
output: PCI passthrough binds the host device to the `vfio-pci` driver, so the VM can use its own drivers for the device. Inside the guest, `lspci` shows the device, although the PCI address may differ from the host's.

instruction: I don't see any PCI Devices page in Harvester. What's missing?
output: Enable the `pcidevices-controller` add-on. After it deploys, scanning can take a few minutes before the PCIDevice objects appear under Advanced > PCI Devices.

instruction: Can I pass through one of the NICs used by the management network?
output: No. Do not pass through host-owned PCI devices such as management and VLAN NICs. Incorrect device allocation can damage the cluster, including causing node failure. Pass through only devices the host does not use.

instruction: What do I need to enable vGPU support in SUSE Virtualization?
output: You need an NVIDIA GPU that supports SR-IOV, the `pcidevices-controller` add-on, and the `nvidia-driver-toolkit` add-on, which manages the vGPU lifecycle. Then enable the GPU on Advanced > SR-IOV GPU Devices, choose a profile on the vGPU Devices screen, and attach the vGPU to a VM.

instruction: In Harvester 1.8, how do I attach a configured vGPU to a VM?
output: Starting with v1.8.0, vGPUs are handled through standard PCI passthrough. Configuring a VGPUDevice automatically enables passthrough of the matching PCIDevice, so attach the PCIDevice that has the same name as the VGPUDevice to the VM.

instruction: How many vGPUs can I get from one GPU in SUSE Virtualization?
output: When vGPU support is enabled on a GPU, the NVIDIA driver creates 16 vGPU devices by default. The profile you choose sets the real maximum: after the first profile is selected the driver adjusts the profiles available for the rest. Once the maximum is reached, the remaining vGPUs cannot be configured.

instruction: Can I give one VM two vGPUs?
output: Sometimes. Not all NVIDIA profiles support multiple vGPUs per VM; for A2 and A16 GPUs, for example, only Q-series profiles do. Also, only one GPU device in the VM definition can have `ramFB` enabled, so add `virtualGPUOptions` with `ramFB` disabled to every non-primary vGPU in the VM YAML.

instruction: How do I import a Harvester cluster into Rancher?
output: In the Rancher UI, open the hamburger menu, choose Virtualization Management and select Import Existing. Enter the cluster name and click Create. Rancher shows a registration guide; follow it on the SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) dashboard, which configures the `cluster-registration-url` setting. When the agent is ready, the cluster appears in Rancher.

instruction: What network access does SUSE Virtualization need for Rancher integration?
output: All SUSE Virtualization nodes must be able to connect to TCP port 443 of the Rancher load balancer. Guest Kubernetes clusters provisioned from Rancher on SUSE Virtualization also need to reach Rancher on TCP 443, or Rancher cannot manage them.

instruction: The import of my Harvester cluster into Rancher is stuck. What should I check?
output: Check the `cattle-cluster-agent-*` pod in `cattle-system`. If it shows `ImagePullBackOff` for `rancher/rancher-agent:<version>`, the cluster cannot pull the agent image, which is not included in the ISO. Configure a private registry or HTTP proxy, or import the image manually, then delete the pod so it is recreated. Also confirm the nodes can reach Rancher on TCP 443.

instruction: Which SUSE Virtualization setting holds the Rancher registration URL?
output: The `cluster-registration-url` setting. Its `url` field holds the Rancher registration URL and `insecureSkipTLSVerify` controls TLS verification, which is not recommended to skip in production. Setting it creates a `cattle-cluster-agent-*` pod in `cattle-system` that uses the `rancher/rancher-agent` image matching the Rancher version.

instruction: Where should I run Rancher to manage our Harvester clusters in production?
output: Install Rancher on a dedicated, high-availability Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes that meets Rancher's requirements. Do not install Rancher with Docker in production, because the environment may be damaged and unrecoverable.

instruction: Can I just docker run Rancher to manage SUSE Virtualization?
output: Only for quick evaluation and testing. The documentation says not to install Rancher with Docker in production. Use a dedicated HA Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes.

instruction: For a lab, is it OK to run Rancher inside a VM on Harvester itself?
output: Yes, for testing. You can create a VM in SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) and install Rancher with Helm (Helm CLI Quick Start) to try the integration. For production, use a dedicated high-availability Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes.

instruction: What's the recommended deployment for the Rancher server that imports SUSE Virtualization?
output: A dedicated high-availability Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes that meets Rancher's software, hardware and networking requirements. Docker-based Rancher installs are for evaluation only.

instruction: How do I create an RKE2 cluster on Harvester from Rancher?
output: First create a cloud credential: Cluster Management > Cloud Credentials > Create > Harvester, select Imported Harvester Cluster, and click Create. Then go to Clusters > Create, toggle the switch to RKE2/K3s, select the Harvester node driver and the credential, and enter the cluster name, namespace, image, network name and SSH user. Click Create.

instruction: Can I use an ISO image with the Harvester node driver?
output: No. The Harvester node driver supports only cloud images. ISO images usually need extra setup that interferes with an unattended deployment.

instruction: What network does a Rancher-provisioned guest cluster on SUSE Virtualization need?
output: The Harvester node driver requires a VLAN network. The VMs get their IP addresses from a DHCP server on that VLAN; if none exists, use the Managed DHCP add-on.

instruction: What do I get from using the Harvester node driver instead of building VMs by hand?
output: Rancher manages the node pools and can create a replacement node automatically when one loses connectivity, keeping the pool at its expected size. The node driver also integrates the Harvester cloud provider for load balancer support and the Harvester CSI driver for storage passthrough to the guest cluster.

instruction: My Rancher guest cluster on Harvester never finishes provisioning. The image is a minimal cloud image. What could it be?
output: The image probably lacks `qemu-guest-agent`. Since Harvester node driver v0.6.3 the agent is not injected automatically, and without it the cluster is not provisioned successfully. Add it in Show Advanced > User Data: a `#cloud-config` with `packages: - qemu-guest-agent` and a `runcmd` that runs `systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent.service`.

instruction: Does the Harvester node driver install the QEMU guest agent for me?
output: Not anymore. Starting with node driver v0.6.3, automatic injection of `qemu-guest-agent` was removed. If the cloud image does not include it, install it through the node driver's User Data cloud-config.

instruction: What user data should I add for RKE2 node pools on SUSE Virtualization?
output: Add a cloud-config that installs and starts the guest agent: `#cloud-config`, `package_update: true`, `packages: - qemu-guest-agent`, and `runcmd` with `systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent.service`. Images without the agent otherwise fail to provision since node driver v0.6.3.

instruction: Why do guest cluster nodes on Harvester get stuck with no IP in Rancher?
output: A common cause is a cloud image without `qemu-guest-agent`, which reports the VM's IP. The Harvester node driver stopped injecting it in v0.6.3, so install it with a User Data cloud-config (`packages: - qemu-guest-agent` and `systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent.service`).

instruction: My Harvester VM is stuck Unschedulable and the pod says no node matches the affinity. Why?
output: SUSE Virtualization automatically adds affinity rules based on the VM definition. A VM attached to cluster network `cn2` gets a rule requiring the node label `network.harvesterhci.io/cn2`. If no active node has set up `cn2`, the virt-launcher pod stays Pending and the VM is Unschedulable. Configure the cluster network on active nodes so they get the label.

instruction: What does the label network.harvesterhci.io/<name> on nodes mean?
output: It marks nodes where the cluster network `<name>` is set up. VMs that use a VM network on that cluster network get an automatic affinity rule requiring the label, so they can only be scheduled or migrated to those nodes.

instruction: I edited a VM's YAML to remove an affinity rule and Harvester put it back. Why?
output: The rule was applied automatically, for example `network.harvesterhci.io/<cluster-network>` for a VM on a custom cluster network. The webhook reverts manual changes to automatically applied rules. Fix the underlying condition by making the cluster network active on the nodes you need.

instruction: A VM on a custom cluster network won't start after its only node with that network went down. What's happening?
output: The VM has an automatically applied affinity rule for its cluster network (`network.harvesterhci.io/<cluster-network>`). With no active node carrying that label, the pod is Pending and the VM is Unschedulable. Bring the node back, or add a network configuration so other active nodes have the cluster network.

instruction: A stopped VM in Harvester has no Start button. How do I fix it?
output: This happens when the VM, VMI and virt-launcher pod all still exist with the pod `Completed`, while the VM status holds a pending `Start` request. Force delete the virt-launcher pod: `kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force`. After the pod is gone, the Start button is visible again.

instruction: Command only: force delete a stuck virt-launcher pod.
output: `kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force`

instruction: How do I tell if the missing Start button problem is the known virt-launcher issue?
output: Run `kubectl get vm`, `kubectl get vmi` and `kubectl get pod` in the namespace. In the known issue the VM shows `Stopped`, the virt-launcher pod shows `Completed`, and the VM's `stateChangeRequests` contains both `Stop` and `Start`. The workaround is `kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force`.

instruction: Users can't power on a VM in SUSE Virtualization; only the Start button is gone. What's the workaround?
output: Force delete the VM's completed virt-launcher pod with `kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force`. The UI hides Start while the VM still has a pending Start request; once the pod is deleted the button returns.

instruction: How do I enable the allow-downgrade setting so I can roll SUSE Virtualization back from v1.8 to v1.7?
output: There is no `allow-downgrade` setting, and SUSE Virtualization does not support downgrades. The restriction prevents problems from incompatible, deprecated or removed functions. Protect yourself before an upgrade instead: back up VMs to a backup target and follow the supported upgrade paths.

instruction: Which Longhorn recurring job should I configure to back up my Harvester VMs every night?
output: None. Recurring Longhorn snapshot and backup jobs are not supported in SUSE Virtualization (Harvester); they conflict with operations such as VM attachment and upgrades and can generate heavy I/O. Use the Virtual Machine Schedules screen: Create Schedule, type Backup, a cron expression with an interval of at least one hour, and a Retain count.

instruction: How do I add a second witness node to my SUSE Virtualization cluster for extra safety?
output: You can't. Each SUSE Virtualization cluster can have only one witness node. The supported layout is two management nodes plus one witness node, optionally with worker nodes. For more resilience, add management-capable nodes instead.

instruction: What's the kubectl command to change an existing Harvester worker node's role to witness?
output: There is no such command. The witness role can be assigned only when a node joins the cluster, by choosing Witness Role in the installer, and each cluster can have only one witness node. To get a witness, remove the node and rejoin it with the Witness Role.

instruction: Which SUSE Virtualization setting turns on nested virtualization so I can run ESXi inside a VM?
output: There is no such setting. Nested virtualization is not supported for guest VMs on SUSE Virtualization; running hypervisors inside its VMs is outside the official support scope. Run hypervisors on supported bare-metal hardware instead.

instruction: How do I set the live-migration-timeout setting in Harvester to 3600 seconds?
output: `live-migration-timeout` is not a SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) setting. Migration timeouts are fields of the `kubevirt-migration` setting: `completionTimeoutPerGiB` (default 150 seconds per GiB) and `progressTimeout` (default 150 seconds). Consider enabling `allowAutoConverge` before raising timeouts.

instruction: How do I set MTU 9000 directly on a VM network in SUSE Virtualization?
output: You can't set the MTU on a VM network directly; the webhook rejects it. VM networks inherit the MTU from the network configuration of their cluster network. Change the MTU on the cluster network's network configuration (with attached VMs stopped), and the VM networks are updated automatically. For `mgmt`, use the `network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu` annotation.

instruction: Can I point the Harvester node driver at an ISO image to build guest cluster nodes?
output: No. The Harvester node driver supports only cloud images. ISO images usually need additional setup that interferes with a clean, unattended deployment. Upload a cloud image (for example a qcow2 cloud image) and select it in the node pool.

instruction: How do I back up a VM whose disks are on our third-party CSI StorageClass using Harvester's Take Backup?
output: That isn't supported. In SUSE Virtualization (Harvester), backup support is limited to SUSE Storage (Longhorn) volumes, and volumes in external storage cannot be backed up. VMs on SUSE Storage can use Take Backup with a backup target set at Settings > backup-target. Protect third-party volumes with the storage vendor's tools.

instruction: Can I upgrade SUSE Virtualization from v1.6.x straight to v1.8.x to save a maintenance window?
output: No, that is not a supported upgrade path. Upgrades move one minor version at a time: v1.6.x to v1.7.x, then v1.7.x to v1.8.x. Within that path you can skip intermediate patch releases. Skipping Kubernetes minor versions is not supported upstream, which is why the paths are limited.

instruction: What's the harvester command to change a node's management IP after installation?
output: There is no documented command for this, because changing a node's IP is not possible during the lifecycle of a SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) cluster. A node whose IP changes cannot join the cluster and might break it. With DHCP, make sure the server always gives the node the same IP.

instruction: What containers make up a SUSE Security deployment?
output: SUSE Security (the NeuVector project) is built from four types of security containers: the Controller, the Enforcer, the Manager and the Scanner. In addition, an Updater container is used to keep the Scanner's CVE database current. Each has a distinct role: the Controller manages policy and the Enforcers, Enforcers apply policy on each node, the Manager provides the web console, and Scanners perform vulnerability and compliance scans.

instruction: I'm new to NeuVector. Can you list its main components?
output: NeuVector, delivered by SUSE as SUSE Security, has four security container types: Controller, Enforcer, Manager and Scanner. There is also an Updater container that triggers CVE database updates for the scanners. Those are the components you will see as pods in the deployment namespace.

instruction: Name the four security container types in SUSE Security.
output: The four security container types are the Controller, the Enforcer, the Manager and the Scanner. An Updater container complements them by updating the CVE database used by the Scanner.

instruction: We're sizing a cluster for SUSE Security. Which pods should I expect it to run?
output: Expect the four SUSE Security container types: Controller, Enforcer, Manager and Scanner, plus the Updater, which runs to refresh the CVE database. The Enforcer runs on every node you want protected, while the Controller, Manager and Scanner run as smaller sets of pods.

instruction: What does the NeuVector controller do?
output: The Controller manages the SUSE Security Enforcer container cluster and provides the REST APIs that the management console uses. Typical test deployments run one Controller, but multiple Controllers in a high-availability configuration are recommended, and the Kubernetes production sample deploys 3 by default.

instruction: How many controllers should I run in production?
output: SUSE Security recommends running multiple Controllers in a high-availability configuration rather than one. The Kubernetes production sample deploys 3 Controllers by default. The Controller is the component that manages the Enforcers and serves the REST API for the console.

instruction: Which SUSE Security component exposes the REST API?
output: The Controller provides the REST APIs, which the management console (Manager) uses. It also manages the cluster of Enforcers. For production, run several Controllers for high availability; 3 is the default in the Kubernetes production sample.

instruction: Is one controller enough for a NeuVector cluster?
output: One Controller is typical for test deployments, but for production SUSE Security recommends multiple Controllers in a high-availability configuration. The Kubernetes production sample yaml uses 3 Controllers. The Controller manages the Enforcers and provides the REST APIs for the console.

instruction: Where does the NeuVector enforcer run?
output: The Enforcer is a lightweight container that enforces SUSE Security policies, and one should run on each node (host). On Kubernetes this is done with a DaemonSet so every node gets an Enforcer.

instruction: What is the job of the enforcer in SUSE Security?
output: The Enforcer enforces the security policies on the host it runs on. It is a lightweight container, and one Enforcer is deployed per node, typically as a DaemonSet.

instruction: A new worker node joined the cluster but nothing is protecting its pods. Which NeuVector component must be on that node?
output: Each node needs a SUSE Security Enforcer, the lightweight container that enforces security policies on that host. Enforcers are normally deployed as a DaemonSet so that every node, including new ones, gets one; check that the Enforcer DaemonSet is scheduling a pod on the new node.

instruction: Should the enforcer be a Deployment or a DaemonSet?
output: The Enforcer should run once on every node (host), so it is deployed as a DaemonSet. It is the lightweight container that enforces the security policies locally.

instruction: What does the NeuVector manager container provide?
output: The Manager is a stateless container that provides the web UI console, served over HTTPS only, for managing SUSE Security. It uses the Controller's REST API behind the scenes.

instruction: Can I put several NeuVector managers behind a load balancer?
output: The SUSE Security docs do not recommend deploying (scaling) more than one Manager behind a load balancer, because of potential session state issues. The Manager is the stateless container that provides the HTTPS web console.

instruction: Users get logged out randomly from the SUSE Security console after we scaled the manager to 3 replicas behind an LB. Why?
output: Scaling more than one Manager behind a load balancer is not recommended because of potential session state issues, which matches the logouts you see. Run a single Manager behind the load balancer. The Manager is the stateless container serving the HTTPS-only web UI.

instruction: Does the SUSE Security console support plain HTTP?
output: The Manager provides the web UI console over HTTPS only. It is a stateless container, and the docs advise against scaling more than one Manager behind a load balancer due to session state issues.

instruction: What does the scanner do in NeuVector?
output: The Scanner performs vulnerability and compliance scanning for images, containers and nodes. It is usually deployed as a replicaset and can be scaled to many parallel scanners; the Controller hands out scan jobs to available scanners round-robin. It also contains the CVE database, which SUSE updates regularly.

instruction: How do I make SUSE Security image scanning faster?
output: Scale out the Scanner. Scanners run as a replicaset and can be scaled up to as many parallel scanners as needed, and the Controller assigns scanning jobs to each available scanner in a round-robin fashion until all scans are completed.

instruction: How are scan jobs distributed when several scanners are running?
output: The Controller assigns scanning jobs to each available Scanner in a round-robin fashion until all scans are done. Scanners are deployed as a replicaset, so you can scale them to increase scanning throughput.

instruction: Which component scans nodes and running containers for CVEs?
output: The Scanner performs vulnerability and compliance scanning for images, containers and nodes. It is deployed as a replicaset and the Controller assigns it jobs round-robin.

instruction: How does NeuVector keep its CVE database up to date?
output: The CVE database lives inside the Scanner image, which SUSE publishes with the 'latest' tag as often as daily. The Updater container restarts the scanner deployment, forcing a pull of the latest scanner image and therefore the newest CVE database. The sample deployments run the Updater as a cron job every day at midnight (schedule "0 0 * * *").

instruction: What is the neuvector-updater-pod cron job for?
output: It runs the Updater, which re-deploys the scanner pods so they pull the latest scanner image containing the newest CVE database. In the sample yaml it runs daily at midnight with the schedule "0 0 * * *", and the schedule can be adjusted.

instruction: Do I need to update the CVE database manually in SUSE Security on Kubernetes?
output: Usually not. The sample Kubernetes deployments start an Updater cron job automatically; it runs every day at midnight ("0 0 * * *") and restarts the scanner deployment so the latest scanner image, and with it the latest CVE database, is pulled.

instruction: Is the CVE database a separate download from the scanner?
output: No. The Scanner image contains the CVE database, and SUSE publishes updated scanner images frequently. To update, the Updater restarts the scanner deployment to force a pull of the latest scanner image; by default this runs as a nightly cron job at midnight.

instruction: Why should NeuVector controllers be an odd number?
output: SUSE Security Controllers use the consensus-based RAFT protocol to elect a leader and to elect a new one if the leader fails. Because of this, run an odd number of active Controllers, for example 3, 5 or 7.

instruction: Can I run 4 controllers for extra redundancy?
output: The docs recommend an odd number of active Controllers, such as 3, 5 or 7, because Controllers use the RAFT consensus protocol for leader election. Use 3 or 5 rather than 4.

instruction: How do SUSE Security controllers pick a leader?
output: Controllers use the consensus-based RAFT protocol to elect a leader, and if the leader goes down they elect another. This is why the recommended Controller count is an odd number like 3, 5 or 7.

instruction: What controller count do you recommend for an HA SUSE Security install?
output: Run multiple Controllers in an odd number, for example 3, 5 or 7. The Controllers use the RAFT consensus protocol for leader election, which is why an odd count is recommended.

instruction: What are the system requirements for SUSE Security components?
output: From the system requirements table: the Controller needs 1 vCPU and 2GB minimum memory (minimum 1 instance, 3 for HA, odd numbers only); the Enforcer needs 1 or more vCPU and 1GB, one per node; the Scanner needs 1 vCPU and 2GB (2 or more for HA/performance); the Manager needs 1 vCPU and 1GB.

instruction: How much memory does the NeuVector enforcer need?
output: The Enforcer's minimum memory is 1GB, with 1 or more vCPU, and one Enforcer runs per node/VM. A dedicated vCPU helps for higher network throughput in Protect mode.

instruction: Minimum memory for the NeuVector controller and scanner?
output: Both the Controller and the Scanner have a 2GB minimum memory recommendation with 1 vCPU. Run at least 3 Controllers (odd number) for HA and 2 or more Scanners for HA or performance.

instruction: We are planning resources for a 10-node RKE2 cluster with SUSE Security. What should each component get?
output: Use the documented minimums: one Enforcer per node with 1+ vCPU and 1GB each (10 Enforcers here), Controllers with 1 vCPU and 2GB each (3 for HA), Scanners with 1 vCPU and 2GB (2 or more for performance), and the Manager with 1 vCPU and 1GB.

instruction: How much memory should the scanner have for big images?
output: The scanner pulls and expands each image in memory. The 2GB minimum assumes images no larger than 0.5GB; for images larger than 1GB, set scanner memory to the largest image size plus 0.5GB. For example, if the largest image is 1.3GB, give the scanner 1.8GB.

instruction: Our scanner pods get OOMKilled scanning ML images. How should I size them?
output: Size scanner memory from your largest image: when images exceed 1GB, the docs say to take the largest image size and add 0.5GB. The scanner expands the image in memory, so a too-small limit fails on big images. Also consider spreading scanners across nodes.

instruction: Is there a formula for NeuVector scanner memory?
output: Yes. For images larger than 1GB, scanner memory = largest image size + 0.5GB, e.g. 1.3GB largest image gives 1.8GB. Below that, the 2GB minimum applies, which assumes images up to 0.5GB.

instruction: Why does the scanner need more RAM than the image size?
output: Registry image scanning pulls the image and expands it in memory inside the scanner. The documented rule for images over 1GB is to allocate the largest image size plus 0.5GB, for example 1.8GB for a 1.3GB image.

instruction: What are the NeuVector protection modes?
output: SUSE Security has three modes: Discover, Monitor and Protect. Any group beginning with 'nv', or the 'Nodes' group, can be in any of them, and the mode can be switched from the Groups menu, Network Activity view or Dashboard.

instruction: Which groups can I put into Protect mode?
output: Learned groups (names beginning with 'nv') and the 'Nodes' group can be set to Discover, Monitor or Protect. Custom groups you create yourself do not have a protection mode, because they may contain containers from different underlying groups in different modes.

instruction: Why is there no mode selector on my custom group?
output: Custom created groups don't have a protection mode in SUSE Security. They may contain containers from different underlying groups, each possibly in a different mode, so a group-level mode would be confusing. Set the mode on the 'nv.' groups instead.

instruction: List the three NeuVector modes.
output: Discover, Monitor and Protect. They apply to 'nv' groups and the 'Nodes' group; custom groups have no protection mode.

instruction: What happens in Discover mode?
output: In Discover mode SUSE Security discovers your containers, nodes and hosts, learns application behaviour by observing network connections, automatically builds a whitelist of network rules and baselines the processes in each service as process profile rules. No blocking happens while learning.

instruction: What mode does NeuVector start new services in?
output: By default SUSE Security starts in Discover mode, and newly discovered services are put into the default New Service Mode, which is Discover unless changed (the ConfigMap setting New_Service_Policy_Mode defaults to Discover). In Discover the service's behaviour is learned and rules are built.

instruction: How do NeuVector network rules get created automatically?
output: They are learned in Discover mode. While a group is in Discover, SUSE Security observes the conversations between containers and automatically creates allow-list network rules, and it also baselines processes into process profile rules.

instruction: We just installed SUSE Security. Will it block anything right away?
output: Not by default. SUSE Security starts in Discover mode, where it learns network connections and processes and builds allow-list rules rather than blocking. New services also default to Discover unless the New Service Mode is changed.

instruction: What does Monitor mode do?
output: In Monitor mode SUSE Security watches conversations and detects run-time violations of your security policy. It does not create new rules (you can still add them manually) and it does not block. Violations appear as red lines in the Network Activity map and are logged in Notifications; process and file violations go to Notifications → Security Events.

instruction: Does Monitor mode block traffic in NeuVector?
output: No. Monitor mode only detects and alerts on violations; blocking happens in Protect mode. In Monitor, no new rules are learned automatically, but you can add rules by hand.

instruction: Where do I see violations while a group is in Monitor mode?
output: Network violations are shown as red lines in the Network Activity map and logged in the Notifications tab. Process profile and file access violations are logged under Notifications → Security Events. Monitor mode alerts but does not block or learn new rules.

instruction: What does Protect mode do in SUSE Security?
output: In Protect mode the Enforcers block (deny) any network violations and attacks detected. Unauthorized processes and file access are also blocked, and matching DLP sensors block network connections. Blocked connections appear in the Network map with a red 'x'.

instruction: Which mode actually blocks traffic in NeuVector?
output: Protect mode. In Protect, Enforcers deny network violations and attacks, and unauthorized processes and file access are blocked. Discover and Monitor do not block policy violations.

instruction: Does Protect mode only cover network traffic?
output: No. Besides blocking network violations and attacks, Protect mode also blocks unauthorized processes and file access. Blocked network connections show a red 'x' in the Network map.

instruction: Pods in one group suddenly can't reach a new backend after I moved the group to Protect. Why?
output: In Protect mode the Enforcers block any connection that is not allowed by a rule. If the new backend connection was never learned or added as a rule, it is denied. Add an allow network rule, or switch the group to Discover to learn the new behaviour before going back to Protect.

instruction: How long should I leave an app in Discover mode?
output: Run test traffic through the application and review the learned rules for completeness. Several hours is usually sufficient, but some applications need a few days to be fully exercised. When in doubt, move to Monitor, look for violations, convert them to whitelist rules, and then go to Protect.

instruction: What's the recommended path from Discover to Protect in NeuVector?
output: Learn in Discover while exercising the application (hours, sometimes days), review the rules, then switch to Monitor and check for violations. Convert legitimate violations into allow rules, and only then move to Protect.

instruction: I'm afraid Protect mode will break my app. How do I roll it out safely?
output: Use Monitor as a checkpoint. After Discover has learned the app with representative test traffic, switch to Monitor, watch for violations, convert valid ones to allow rules, and move to Protect once violations stop. Some applications need a few days in Discover to be fully exercised.

instruction: Before I deploy a release that adds new service connections, what should I do with the group mode?
output: Switch the affected services to Discover mode before the update so the new connections are learned. Alternatively, add the new rules manually in any mode or update the CRD that defines them. Then return to Monitor or Protect after reviewing.

instruction: Which mode wins when a Protect group talks to a Monitor group?
output: The least restrictive mode wins. A connection between a Protect group and a Monitor group is evaluated as Monitor, so it is alerted but not blocked. This conflict resolution applies only to network rules.

instruction: How does NeuVector resolve mode conflicts between source and destination?
output: For network connections between groups in different modes, the effective mode is always the least restrictive one. For example, Discover with anything gives Discover, and Monitor with Protect gives Monitor. This only applies to network rules.

instruction: My frontend is in Protect but a bad connection from it to a Discover-mode database wasn't blocked. Why?
output: Connections between groups in different modes use the least restrictive mode. Protect to Discover resolves to Discover, so the connection is learned rather than blocked. Put both groups in Protect if you want the connection enforced.

instruction: In what order are NeuVector network rules evaluated?
output: SUSE Security network rules are enforced in the order they appear in the list, from top to bottom. You can re-order a rule with the 'Move to' option. Remember that edits are not applied until you click Save at the top.

instruction: What happens to a connection that matches no network rule?
output: The default action is Deny. In Monitor mode the connection is logged as a violation; in Protect mode it is blocked.

instruction: I added a network rule but nothing changed. What did I miss?
output: Network rule edits (add, delete, change) are not applied until you click the Save/Deploy button at the top of the page; leaving the page without deploying loses them. Also check the rule's position, since rules are enforced top to bottom.

instruction: Is NeuVector network policy default-allow or default-deny?
output: Default deny. If no rule matches a connection, the action is Deny: a violation is logged in Monitor mode and the connection is blocked in Protect mode. Rules are matched top to bottom.

instruction: How do I allow a pod to talk to a database outside the cluster in NeuVector?
output: Create a group for the destination, then a rule for it. In Policy → Groups add a custom group (for example 'internal') with criteria such as the DNS name, IP address or address range of the service. Then in Policy → Network Rules add a rule from the source group to that group, set it to Allow, and click Deploy. Check the rule order afterwards.

instruction: Traffic to our on-prem LDAP server shows as 'External'. How do I write a rule for it?
output: SUSE Security classifies networks it does not manage as External. Define a custom group with address criteria for the LDAP server (DNS name, IP or range), then add an Allow network rule from your application group to that group and deploy it.

instruction: What is the documented way to do egress control to internal services on another subnet?
output: Two steps: (1) create a custom group in Policy → Groups whose criteria are the internal service's DNS name, IP address or address range; (2) create an Allow rule from the originating group to this new group, optionally narrowed by protocol or port, and Deploy. Rules apply top to bottom, so verify placement.

instruction: Can I target an external IP range in a network rule?
output: Yes, through an address group. Create a custom group with an address criterion such as address=10.1.0.0/24, then use that group as the To side of an Allow network rule and deploy.

instruction: After setting externalTrafficPolicy Local, NeuVector flags ingress traffic as external and blocks it. How do I fix that?
output: SUSE Security uses the X-Forwarded-For header to recognise the original source IP, so traffic is now identified as coming from 'external' and can violate rules that expected the ingress or proxy as source. Either adjust your rules, or go to Settings → Configuration and disable 'X-Forwarded-For based policy match', which is enabled by default.

instruction: Is X-Forwarded-For used in NeuVector policy enforcement?
output: Yes, by default. SUSE Security can read X-Forwarded-For headers added by load balancers and ingress controllers to identify the real source IP and enforce policy on it. It can be disabled with the 'X-Forwarded-For based policy match' setting in Settings → Configuration.

instruction: Where is the switch to stop NeuVector using X-Forwarded-For?
output: Settings → Configuration, setting 'X-Forwarded-For based policy match'. Disabling it tells SUSE Security not to identify connections as external based on X-Forwarded-For headers.

instruction: Can NeuVector block network traffic on the nodes themselves?
output: No. Network connection violations of rules for the 'nodes' group are never blocked, even in Protect mode. On nodes, only process violations are blocked in Protect mode.

instruction: What is the 'nodes' group in SUSE Security?
output: It is a group created automatically to represent each node (host) in the cluster. SUSE Security monitors hosts for suspicious processes and privilege escalations and learns node processes in Discover mode. In Protect mode only process violations are blocked on nodes; network violations are never blocked.

instruction: How do I turn on host protection in NeuVector?
output: Select the 'nodes' group, review the learned process rules (the list combines processes from all nodes while in Discover), edit if needed, then switch the group to Monitor or Protect. Note that in Protect only process violations are blocked on nodes; network violations for nodes are never blocked.

instruction: Is zero-drift the default process protection in SUSE Security?
output: It depends on the version. Zero-drift was the default for process and file protection in NeuVector 5.6.0 and older. Starting from NeuVector 5.6.1, Basic mode is the default in new deployments. Check your version before assuming either.

instruction: What changed about process protection defaults in NeuVector 5.6.1?
output: From 5.6.1, new deployments default to Basic process/file protection instead of zero-drift (the 5.6.1 release notes describe reverting zero-drift for processes to not be the default). In 5.6.0 and older, zero-drift was the default.

instruction: On a fresh 5.6.2 install, which process protection mode will my groups use?
output: For new deployments starting from NeuVector 5.6.1, Basic is the default process/file protection mode, so a fresh 5.6.2 install uses Basic. Zero-drift can be enabled per group in Policy → Groups.

instruction: What is zero-drift in NeuVector?
output: Zero-drift is a process and file protection that automatically allows only processes originating from the parent process in the original container image, and does not allow file updates or new files to be installed. It does not require processes to be learned or added to an allow-list. In Discover or Monitor mode it alerts on suspicious activity; in Protect mode it blocks it.

instruction: Does zero-drift need a learning period?
output: No. Zero-drift does not require processes to be learned or added to an allow-list; allowed activity is determined from the original container image. Any process or file activity outside that is alerted in Discover/Monitor and blocked in Protect.

instruction: Someone ran apt-get install inside a container with zero-drift in Protect mode. What happens?
output: Zero-drift does not allow file updates or new files to be installed, so in Protect mode that activity is blocked; in Discover or Monitor mode it would only be alerted. Processes not originating from the image's original parent process are treated the same way.

instruction: How do I add exceptions when zero-drift is enabled?
output: The process and file rules listed for a group are always applied, even with zero-drift enabled, so you add allow or deny rules to the group as exceptions. Review any rules auto-added while the group was in Discover before moving to Monitor or Protect.

instruction: How does Basic process protection work in SUSE Security?
output: Basic protection enforces process and file activity according to the process and/or file rules listed for each group. Rules can come from behavioural learning in Discover mode, manual creation in the console or REST API, or a CRD. If a group uses Basic and has no rules, all activity is alerted (Monitor) or blocked (Protect).

instruction: I switched a group to Basic and Protect and every process is blocked. Why?
output: With Basic protection, enforcement relies entirely on the group's process/file rules. If no rules are in place, all activity is alerted or blocked in Monitor or Protect mode. Let the group learn in Discover mode first or add rules manually or via CRD.

instruction: Where do Basic-mode process rules come from?
output: Three ways: auto-created through behavioural learning while the group is in Discover mode, created manually through the console or REST API, or created programmatically by applying a CRD.

instruction: Our debugging pod runs nmap and NeuVector keeps alerting even in Discover mode. Why isn't it learned?
output: nmap is one of the built-in suspicious processes. Suspicious processes such as nmap or ncat are reported as suspicious process events and are not learned, even in Discover mode. If the service genuinely needs it, add a process profile rule with an explicit 'allow' for it.

instruction: Does Discover mode learn every process?
output: All new processes are profiled with action allow in Discover mode, except built-in suspicious processes (for example nmap, ncat, reverse shells). Those are reported as suspicious events and not learned; they need an explicit allow rule.

instruction: How do I stop alerts for ncat that our app legitimately uses?
output: Add an explicit 'allow' process profile rule for ncat in that group. Built-in suspicious processes like ncat and nmap are never learned automatically, so the allow rule is required.

instruction: Can NeuVector block changes to /etc/passwd inside a container?
