instruction: Which SUSE Linux BCI contains no GPLv3 software?
output: SUSE Linux BCI-BusyBox. Its basic tools are provided by BusyBox, and the image contains no GPLv3-licensed software. It is also very small, about 12 MB for the 15.7 tag.

instruction: My shell script works on bci-base but fails on bci-busybox. Why?
output: BCI-BusyBox uses BusyBox implementations of the basic tools instead of GNU Coreutils, and there are differences between them. It also has no bash. Scripts written for a GNU Coreutils system may need changes to work with BusyBox.

instruction: When should I use bci-busybox?
output: Use it when you need a very small image and no GPLv3-licensed software. It ships only basic BusyBox tools, without bash, rpm or Zypper, so check that your scripts work with BusyBox tools.

instruction: Is bash available in the SUSE Linux BCI-BusyBox image?
output: No. According to the BCI support matrix, BCI-BusyBox has glibc, CA certificates and the RPM database, and BusyBox provides its tools; bash, rpm and Zypper are not included.

instruction: Do I need a SUSE subscription to use SUSE Linux BCIs?
output: No. SUSE Linux BCIs do not require a subscription to run or distribute. A permissive EULA lets you redistribute custom images built on them. Support is available through SUSE subscription plans if you want it.

instruction: Can I publish an image based on bci-base on a public registry?
output: Yes. SUSE Linux Base Container Images are covered by a permissive EULA that allows redistributing custom container images based on them, and no subscription is needed to run or distribute them.

instruction: What is the SLE_BCI repository?
output: It is a free repository, one per SLES service pack (for example SLE_BCI 15 SP7), that is a subset of the SLE repository. It gives SUSE Linux BCIs access to over 4000 packages for AMD64/Intel 64, AArch64, POWER and IBM Z. It contains all SLE packages except items such as kernels, boot loaders, installers and desktop environments.

instruction: Our devs run containers on macOS laptops, not SLES. Can they still use SUSE Linux BCIs?
output: Yes. BCIs don't require a subscription to run or distribute, and Zypper-based BCIs use the free SLE_BCI repository. Access to the full SLES repositories through container-suseconnect only works on a registered SLES host; elsewhere that plugin does nothing.

instruction: Should I use registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:latest in my Dockerfile?
output: SUSE recommends against relying on `:latest` for reproducible builds. Pin an explicit version tag instead, for example `FROM registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7` for SLES 15 SP7, or the relevant 16.x tag for SUSE Linux 16. The `:latest` tag is migrating from SLES 15 to SUSE Linux 16 image by image, so it could silently change your base.

instruction: Is bci-base:latest SLES 15 or 16?
output: The BCI family is moving `:latest` to SUSE Linux 16 in stages. bci-nano moved first, and bci-base, bci-init, bci-minimal, bci-micro and bci-busybox follow later. Until each switch, `bci-base:latest` still gives a 15 SP7-based image. Check `/etc/os-release` in the image, and pin `:15.7` or a 16.x tag to be sure.

instruction: How long are the SLES 15 SP7 BCIs maintained?
output: SLES 15 SP7-based SUSE Linux BCIs remain maintained until the end of general support for SP7, 31 July 2031. To stay on them, pin the `15.7` tag, for example `registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7`.

instruction: Our CI broke after a base image changed underneath us. How should we reference SUSE BCIs?
output: Pin an explicit version tag in your FROM lines, CI pipelines and pull commands, for example `registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7`, rather than `:latest`. SUSE is moving `:latest` across the BCI family to SUSE Linux 16, and pinning prevents that change from altering your deployments.

instruction: How can I check whether a SUSE Linux BCI tag is fully supported?
output: Read its `com.suse.supportlevel` label. With skopeo and jq, you don't need to pull the image: `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`. A value of `l3` means full SUSE support; `techpreview` means the image is unsupported and meant for proofs of concept. Always check the exact tag you use.

instruction: Just the command to read the supportlevel label of bci-base:15.7 without pulling it.
output: `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`

instruction: What do the values of com.suse.supportlevel mean?
output: `l2` means problem isolation and `l3` means problem resolution, with engineering engaged. `acc` means the software may require an external contract, `techpreview` means unsupported and intended for proofs of concept, and `unsupported` means no support. Check a tag with `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`.

instruction: Is the label check something I should repeat per tag?
output: Yes. The value can differ between service packs (an older tag may be out of support) and between images (a new image may be techpreview). Check each tag you consume, for example `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`.

instruction: What language stack images does SUSE provide as BCIs?
output: Development Stack SUSE Linux BCIs include python, node, openjdk and openjdk-devel, ruby, rust, golang and gcc. They also include dotnet-runtime, dotnet-aspnet and dotnet-sdk, plus php, php-apache and php-fpm. Each is built on BCI-Base with Zypper and the SLE_BCI repository and adds the compiler or interpreter and the language package manager. Check SUSE Registry for currently published tags.

instruction: How long is a Development Stack BCI like python supported?
output: Unlike the general-purpose BCIs, Development Stack BCIs may not follow the SLES lifecycle. They are supported as long as the respective language stack receives support, so new version tags can appear and older ones can become unsupported during a service pack. Pin an explicit version tag and check the support level on SUSE Registry.

instruction: Does the SUSE node BCI include yarn?
output: The node BCI ships nodejs (version from the tag), npm and git. Yarn is not included, but you can install it with `npm install -g yarn`.

instruction: Which BCI should I use to compile C/C++ code?
output: Use the gcc Development Stack BCI, which ships the GNU Compiler Collection (C, C++, Fortran) and build tooling. SUSE suggests pairing it with a smaller deployment image, such as BCI-Micro, in a multi-stage build.

instruction: How do I log in to registry.suse.com to pull LTSS container images with a registration code?
output: Use the literal user name `regcode` and your registration code as the password: `echo SCC_REGISTRATION_CODE | podman login -u "regcode" --password-stdin registry.suse.com`. SUSE suggests wrapping it in `set +o history` and `set -o history` so the code isn't stored in shell history. You need a valid LTSS subscription for these images.

instruction: Command only: podman login to SUSE Registry using an SCC registration code.
output: `echo SCC_REGISTRATION_CODE | podman login -u "regcode" --password-stdin registry.suse.com`

instruction: What other credentials can I use for LTSS images on registry.suse.com besides a registration code?
output: On a registered host, you can use the username and password from `/etc/zypp/credentials.d/SCCcredentials`. You can also use the organization mirroring credentials, which are highly privileged and best kept for a private mirroring registry. With a registration code, log in as `echo SCC_REGISTRATION_CODE | podman login -u "regcode" --password-stdin registry.suse.com`.

instruction: Pulling an LTSS BCI tag fails with unauthorized. What's missing?
output: LTSS container images need a valid LTSS subscription, and you must log in to SUSE Registry first. With a registration code, run `echo SCC_REGISTRATION_CODE | podman login -u "regcode" --password-stdin registry.suse.com`. Then pull the image again.

instruction: How do I log Helm in to SUSE Application Collection?
output: Run `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>`. With a user account, use your username and an access token created under Settings > Access tokens. With a service account, use its username and secret. You can then pull charts such as `oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/...`.

instruction: Command only: helm login for dp.apps.rancher.io.
output: `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>`

instruction: helm pull oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis says unauthorized. What should I run first?
output: Most Application Collection operations need authentication. Log Helm in to the Distribution Platform with `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>`, using an access token or a service account secret. Then retry the pull.

instruction: Can I use my SCC password with helm registry login for Application Collection?
output: For the Distribution Platform, a user account authenticates with its username and an access token, and a service account with its username and secret: `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>`. Create the access token in the Application Collection web application under Settings > Access tokens.

instruction: How do I let Kubernetes pull images from SUSE Application Collection?
output: Create a pull secret for the Distribution Platform: `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection --docker-server=dp.apps.rancher.io --docker-username=<your-username-or-sa-username> --docker-password=<access-token-or-sa-secret>`. Reference it from workloads as an imagePullSecret, or with Application Collection Helm charts, pass `--set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`.

instruction: Give me the kubectl command for the Application Collection image pull secret.
output: `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection --docker-server=dp.apps.rancher.io --docker-username=<your-username-or-sa-username> --docker-password=<access-token-or-sa-secret>`

instruction: Pods using dp.apps.rancher.io/containers images are stuck in ImagePullBackOff. What's missing?
output: The cluster needs credentials for the Distribution Platform. Create the secret with `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection --docker-server=dp.apps.rancher.io --docker-username=<your-username-or-sa-username> --docker-password=<access-token-or-sa-secret>` (add `-n <namespace>` for the workload's namespace). Then reference it as an imagePullSecret.

instruction: What credentials go into the application-collection Kubernetes secret?
output: Your Application Collection username with an access token, or a service account's username with its secret: `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection --docker-server=dp.apps.rancher.io --docker-username=<your-username-or-sa-username> --docker-password=<access-token-or-sa-secret>`. For machine-to-machine use, SUSE recommends a service account.

instruction: How do I install a Helm chart from SUSE Application Collection?
output: Install it from the OCI registry and pass the pull secret through the standardized option, for example `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`. Use `--version` to pick a specific chart version. Run `helm show values oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis` to see all options.

instruction: Command only: install the Redis chart from Application Collection with the pull secret.
output: `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`

instruction: What does --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection} do in Application Collection installs?
output: It tells the chart to pull all its container images with the named Kubernetes pull secret. The option name is standardized across all Application Collection charts, as in `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`.

instruction: My Application Collection chart installed but the pods can't pull images. What option did I probably miss?
output: You probably didn't pass the pull secret to the chart. Reinstall with the standardized option, for example `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imagePullSecrets={application-collection}`. The secret must already exist in the namespace you deploy to.

instruction: Should I use a user account or a service account for Application Collection in CI?
output: Use a service account. SUSE recommends service accounts for machine-to-machine interaction, and they generally have less restrictive rate limits than user accounts. A service account authenticates with its username and secret and belongs to a single organization.

instruction: Why can't my service account pull a SUSE AI chart when my user account can?
output: A service account belongs to one organization and only has that organization's subscriptions. A user account inherits the subscriptions of all organizations the user belongs to. If the service account's organization has no SUSE AI subscription, it can't pull content that requires one.

instruction: Who can create Application Collection service accounts?
output: Only admins of an organization can create service accounts for it. They do this in the web application under Settings > Service accounts, choosing the target organization. The secret is shown once in a green box at creation time.

instruction: How do I get credentials for the Application Collection Distribution Platform as an individual?
output: Sign in to the web application with your SUSE Customer Center account, open Settings > Access tokens, and create a token. You then authenticate with your username and that access token. You can create several tokens and delete any one without affecting the others.

instruction: I created the application-collection secret in default but installed the chart in another namespace and pulls fail. Why?
output: The image pull secret must already be present in the target namespace where the Helm chart is deployed. Create it in that namespace too, for example by adding `-n <namespace>` to `kubectl create secret docker-registry application-collection ...`, then reinstall or upgrade the release.

instruction: How do I point an Application Collection chart at our internal mirror registry?
output: Use the standardized `global.imageRegistry` option, usually together with `global.imagePullSecrets` for the mirror's credentials. For example: `helm install redis oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/redis --set global.imageRegistry=registry.internal --set global.imagePullSecrets={my-custom-oci-registry}`.

instruction: Is global.imageRegistry specific to some charts?
output: No. All Helm charts in SUSE Application Collection include standardized options: `global.imagePullSecrets` for pull secrets and `global.imageRegistry` for overriding the registry of all images, for example when you mirror to a private registry. Each image also supports registry, repository and tag overrides.

instruction: ImagePullBackOff after helm install from dp.apps.rancher.io even though I passed global.imagePullSecrets. What should I check?
output: Check that the named secret exists in the same namespace as the release. The pull secret must already be present in the target namespace, and a secret in a different namespace is not used.

instruction: Does SUSE Rancher Prime include access to the SUSE AI charts?
output: No. The SUSE AI entitlement is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime. After you obtain it, the entitlement check at https://apps.rancher.io/ grants access to pull and deploy the SUSE AI Helm charts and container images in SUSE Application Collection.

instruction: What's the first step in the SUSE AI 1.0 AI Library installation procedure?
output: Obtain the SUSE AI entitlement, which is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime, and verify it at https://apps.rancher.io/. Then sign in to SUSE Application Collection, get a user access token, and create the namespace and pull secrets.

instruction: I can pull Application Collection charts but not the SUSE AI ones like Open WebUI. Why?
output: SUSE AI content needs the SUSE AI entitlement, which is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime. Check the entitlement at https://apps.rancher.io/. Also, if you use a service account, its organization must hold the SUSE AI subscription.

instruction: Where are SUSE AI Library applications distributed from?
output: Their Helm charts and images are hosted in SUSE Application Collection (dp.apps.rancher.io) and SUSE Registry (registry.suse.com). Access to the SUSE AI content requires the SUSE AI entitlement, which is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime.

instruction: Which operating systems does the SUSE AI deployment guide recommend for cluster nodes?
output: SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP6 if you want a traditional non-transactional OS, or SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 if you want an immutable transactional OS. The full list of supported systems is in the SUSE Rancher Prime support matrix.

instruction: Which Kubernetes distribution should I use for SUSE AI?
output: The guide recommends the supported SUSE Rancher Prime: RKE2 distribution. Install and register the OS on each node, install NVIDIA GPU drivers on GPU nodes, then install RKE2.

instruction: What are the base layers of a SUSE AI deployment from scratch?
output: Install and register a supported Linux OS on each node: SLES 15 SP6 (non-transactional) or SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 (transactional). Install the NVIDIA GPU driver on GPU nodes. Then install Kubernetes, preferably SUSE Rancher Prime: RKE2, before preparing the cluster and installing AI Library applications.

instruction: Is SUSE Linux Micro an option for SUSE AI GPU nodes?
output: Yes. The SUSE AI guide recommends SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 for an immutable transactional OS, alongside SLES 15 SP6 for a traditional one. On Micro, the NVIDIA driver is installed inside a `transactional-update shell` session followed by a reboot.

instruction: Can I run Rancher, SUSE Observability and the AI workloads in one cluster for production SUSE AI?
output: SUSE strongly recommends against it for production. Deploy Rancher, SUSE Observability and the AI Library workloads to separate Kubernetes clusters.

instruction: What's the recommended cluster layout for a production SUSE AI install?
output: Use separate Kubernetes clusters for SUSE Rancher Prime (management), SUSE Observability, and the AI Library workloads such as Ollama, Open WebUI and vLLM. SUSE strongly recommends this separation for production.

instruction: For a lab I put everything on one RKE2 cluster. What changes for production SUSE AI?
output: For production, SUSE strongly recommends splitting Rancher, SUSE Observability and the AI Library workloads into separate Kubernetes clusters. A single cluster is fine for experiments but does not follow the production guidance.

instruction: Where should SUSE Observability run relative to the SUSE AI workloads?
output: In its own cluster. The SUSE AI deployment guide strongly recommends deploying Rancher, SUSE Observability and AI Library workloads to separate Kubernetes clusters for production.

instruction: What pull secrets does SUSE AI need in its namespace?
output: Two. Create the `application-collection` secret for dp.apps.rancher.io with your Application Collection username and token. Also create the SUSE Registry secret: `kubectl create secret docker-registry suse-ai-registry --docker-server=registry.suse.com --docker-username=regcode --docker-password=<SCC_REG_CODE> -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`. For SUSE Registry, the username is the literal `regcode`, and the password is the SCC registration code of your SUSE AI subscription.

instruction: Command only: create the SUSE Registry pull secret for SUSE AI.
output: `kubectl create secret docker-registry suse-ai-registry --docker-server=registry.suse.com --docker-username=regcode --docker-password=<SCC_REG_CODE> -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`

instruction: Some SUSE AI images pull from registry.suse.com and fail with unauthorized. What did I skip?
output: You need a pull secret for SUSE Registry as well as for Application Collection: `kubectl create secret docker-registry suse-ai-registry --docker-server=registry.suse.com --docker-username=regcode --docker-password=<SCC_REG_CODE> -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`. Also log Helm in with `helm registry login registry.suse.com -u regcode -p <SCC_REG_CODE>`.

instruction: What username do I use for registry.suse.com in the SUSE AI install?
output: The literal string `regcode`, with your SUSE AI subscription's SCC registration code as the password. For example: `kubectl create secret docker-registry suse-ai-registry --docker-server=registry.suse.com --docker-username=regcode --docker-password=<SCC_REG_CODE> -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`.

instruction: How do I mark GPU nodes for SUSE AI workloads?
output: Label them, for example `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME> accelerator=nvidia-gpu`. Then set `nodeSelector: accelerator: nvidia-gpu` in the chart's values.yaml so the pods schedule only on those nodes. Verify the labels with `kubectl get nodes --show-labels`.

instruction: Give me the kubectl command to label a GPU node the way the SUSE AI guide does.
output: `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME> accelerator=nvidia-gpu`

instruction: Ollama keeps landing on my CPU-only worker. How do I keep it on the GPU nodes?
output: Label the GPU nodes with `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME> accelerator=nvidia-gpu` and add `nodeSelector: accelerator: nvidia-gpu` to Ollama's values. Also request `nvidia.com/gpu` in its resources and enable GPU in the chart.

instruction: Can I label several GPU nodes in one command?
output: Yes. List several node names before the label, as in `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME1> <GPU_NODE_NAME2> accelerator=nvidia-gpu`. For a single node, use `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME> accelerator=nvidia-gpu`. Check with `kubectl get nodes --show-labels`.

instruction: How does a SUSE AI Helm chart request a GPU?
output: Request the `nvidia.com/gpu` resource provided by the NVIDIA GPU Operator, for example `resources: requests: nvidia.com/gpu: 1` and `limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1` in values.yaml. Set the number to match your setup.

instruction: My Ollama pod runs but uses CPU only. What's wrong?
output: Containers are isolated from the host by default, so the chart must enable GPU passthrough. Without it, the container still runs but uses only the CPU. Enable GPU in the Ollama chart values and request `nvidia.com/gpu` in its resources.

instruction: Which resource name does the GPU Operator expose for scheduling?
output: `nvidia.com/gpu`. Once the operator is configured on a node, `kubectl get node $NODENAME -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}'` should show `"nvidia.com/gpu":` with the number of GPUs, and pods request it in their resources.

instruction: Is a nodeSelector enough to give a SUSE AI app a GPU?
output: No. A nodeSelector like `accelerator: nvidia-gpu` only places the pod on a GPU node. To actually get a GPU, request `nvidia.com/gpu` in resources and enable GPU passthrough in the chart.

instruction: How do I check that the GPU Operator detected my host-installed NVIDIA driver on RKE2?
output: Run `kubectl get node $NODENAME -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | grep "nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver"`. The value should be `pre-installed`. If it is `true`, the drivers were not correctly installed; you may have forgotten to reboot the node after installing the packages.

instruction: nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver shows true instead of pre-installed. What does it mean?
output: It means the operator didn't detect correctly installed host drivers. Check the host with `lsmod | grep nvidia`, `cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version`, and `find /usr/ -iname libnvidia-ml.so`. A common cause is not rebooting after installing the driver packages.

instruction: Why did RKE2 restart when I installed the NVIDIA GPU Operator?
output: That is expected. The SUSE AI guide warns that the NVIDIA operator restarts containerd with a hangup call, which restarts RKE2.

instruction: Which host checks should pass before installing the GPU Operator for SUSE AI?
output: `lsmod | grep nvidia` should list the nvidia kernel modules, and `cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version` should show the NVRM and GCC versions. `find /usr/ -iname libnvidia-ml.so` should return the library path. After the operator is installed, `nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver` should read `pre-installed`.

instruction: How do I install the NVIDIA driver on a SUSE Linux Micro GPU node for SUSE AI?
output: Open a `transactional-update shell` to get a read/write snapshot. Inside it, add the NVIDIA CUDA repository and install the open driver KMP (G06 generation for modern GPUs) with zypper. Then `exit`, `reboot`, and run `nvidia-smi` as root to confirm the GPU is detected.

instruction: Why does the SUSE AI guide use transactional-update shell for NVIDIA drivers on Micro?
output: SUSE Linux Micro's root file system is immutable. `transactional-update shell` creates a new read/write snapshot in which zypper can add the NVIDIA repository and install the driver packages. The changes become active after you exit and reboot into that snapshot.

instruction: After installing the NVIDIA packages on SUSE Linux Micro, nvidia-smi isn't found. What did I miss?
output: The packages were installed into a new snapshot from `transactional-update shell`, so they are only active after you `exit` the shell and `reboot`. After the reboot, run `nvidia-smi` as root to check the GPU.

instruction: Which NVIDIA driver generation does the SUSE AI guide install?
output: It documents the G06 generation, which it calls the most common choice for modern GPUs. Verify the right generation for your GPU first. On SUSE Linux Micro, the installation happens inside `transactional-update shell` followed by a reboot.

instruction: What components make up the SUSE AI Library?
output: The SUSE AI 1.0 guide covers cert-manager, a vector database for Open WebUI (OpenSearch or Milvus), Ollama, Open WebUI, vLLM, mcpo, PyTorch, Qdrant, LiteLLM, MLflow and Kubeflow. Install applications with the fewest dependencies first. You can install them individually with Helm, with the SUSE AI Deployer meta chart, or with SUSE AI Lifecycle Manager.

instruction: Do I still get cert-manager automatically with Open WebUI in SUSE AI?
output: No. In earlier releases, cert-manager was installed with Open WebUI, but it is no longer part of the Open WebUI Helm chart. Install it separately from `oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/cert-manager` before the other components.

instruction: Is Ollama installed separately from Open WebUI in SUSE AI?
output: By default, the Open WebUI installation also installs Ollama. If you install Ollama separately with its own chart, disable it in the Open WebUI override file.

instruction: Which vector databases can Open WebUI use in SUSE AI?
output: The SUSE AI guide says Open WebUI supports either OpenSearch or Milvus, and you install one of them as the application with vector database capabilities. Qdrant is also available in the AI Library.

instruction: How do I install Ollama for SUSE AI with Helm?
output: After setting up access, the namespace and the Helm registry login, create an override file and run `helm upgrade --install ollama oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE> -f ollama_custom_overrides.yaml`. To see the chart's options, run `helm show values oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama`.

instruction: Command only: deploy the SUSE AI Ollama chart with my overrides file.
output: `helm upgrade --install ollama oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE> -f ollama_custom_overrides.yaml`

instruction: I want Ollama standalone rather than bundled with Open WebUI in SUSE AI. What do I run?
output: Disable Ollama in the Open WebUI override file, then install Ollama on its own: `helm upgrade --install ollama oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE> -f ollama_custom_overrides.yaml`. Put GPU and model settings in `ollama_custom_overrides.yaml`.

instruction: Where does the SUSE AI Ollama chart come from?
output: From SUSE Application Collection at `oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama`. Install it with `helm upgrade --install ollama oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE> -f ollama_custom_overrides.yaml` after logging Helm in to dp.apps.rancher.io.

instruction: How do I run zypper install directly on SUSE Linux Micro without transactional-update?
output: You can't. SUSE Linux Micro uses a read-only root file system, so you cannot change it directly with `zypper`. The documented way is `sudo transactional-update pkg install package_name`, which installs into a new snapshot that becomes active after a reboot.

instruction: What option makes transactional-update apply a package to the running system immediately, without a reboot?
output: There is no such option. transactional-update always makes its changes in a separate snapshot that does not affect the running system, and the changes become active only after you reboot into it. To batch several changes before one reboot, use `--continue` or `transactional-update shell`.

instruction: Which SUSEConnect flag makes it install the default packages of a module when I activate it?
output: There isn't one. SUSEConnect only registers or deregisters modules and extensions and enables or disables their repositories; it does not install or remove packages. Install packages afterwards with `zypper` or YaST > Software Management, or use YaST to manage modules if you want packages handled automatically.

instruction: Does plain zypper patch also apply patches from third-party repositories?
output: No. Plain `zypper patch` does not apply patches from third-party repositories. To include them, the documented option is `sudo zypper patch --with-update`.

instruction: How do I enable Docker Content Trust / Notary to verify SUSE BCI images from registry.suse.com?
output: Notary v1 / Docker Content Trust is no longer used for SUSE BCIs; its deprecation on SUSE Registry was announced in February 2026. SUSE Linux BCIs are signed with Sigstore Cosign and Podman's GPG signatures, so verify them with one of those mechanisms instead.

instruction: How do I run zypper inside a bci-micro container to add a package?
output: You can't. SUSE Linux BCI-Micro ships neither Zypper nor the rpm binary, and there is no straightforward way to install additional dependencies in it. If you need to install packages, build on SUSE Linux BCI-Base (`registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7`), which includes Zypper and the free SLE_BCI repository, or copy a self-contained binary into BCI-Micro in a multi-stage build.

instruction: My entrypoint uses #!/bin/bash. Does SUSE Linux BCI-BusyBox ship bash?
output: No. According to the BCI support matrix, BCI-BusyBox does not include bash; its basic tools come from BusyBox. Rewrite the script for the BusyBox shell and tools, or use BCI-Micro or BCI-Base, which include bash.

instruction: Is the SUSE AI entitlement automatically included with a SUSE Rancher Prime subscription?
output: No. The SUSE AI 1.0 documentation states that the SUSE AI entitlement is separate from SUSE Rancher Prime. After you obtain it, the entitlement check at https://apps.rancher.io/ gives access to the SUSE AI Helm charts and images in SUSE Application Collection.

instruction: Can I set up Ray or the LoraController with the SUSE AI vLLM chart?
output: No. The SUSE AI documentation states that the current release of SUSE AI vLLM does not support Ray or LoraController. The chart deploys the vLLM production stack (serving engine, router, and optionally LMCache and a cache server) and requires NVIDIA GPUs in the cluster.

instruction: What's the default root password login for Cockpit on a new SUSE Linux Micro install?
output: There is none: on new SUSE Linux Micro installations, root login to Cockpit with a password is disabled by default. Log in with an unprivileged local user and unlock administrative access with the root password. SUSE strongly discourages it, but you can allow root by removing it from `/etc/cockpit/disallowed-users`.

instruction: Can I log in to dp.apps.rancher.io with helm using my SUSE Customer Center password?
output: That is not the documented method. For the Distribution Platform, a user account authenticates with its username and an access token (created under Settings > Access tokens in the web application), and a service account with its username and secret: `helm registry login dp.apps.rancher.io -u <your-username-or-sa-username> -p <access-token-or-sa-secret>`. Your SCC credentials are used to sign in to the web application.
